new_statements.quote: From Menovshchikov (1975) and the tape, we can easily confirm the basics—for example, that there is alternating stress as in anə́ŋaq 'older brother', anə́łxutə́kułɣ́i[i]t 'group of brothers', where clearly ə can bear stress as well as i a u (as in CSY and Norton Sound CAY). There are also plenty of instances of perturbation of this pattern by long vowels ... Here, though, the alternate stress operates usually starting on the second syllable, also the one which Menovshchikov more often chooses to note as more prominent, according to the fundamentally deuterotonic pattern. Sometimes, however, the stress does indeed appear to have fallen definitively on the first syllable, e.g. qántaɣakun, mántiɣamun, where closed initial syllable weight has attracted the stress as in Alaskan Yupik.

First part is p. 185 para 2 ('From Menovshchikov (1975) and the tape, we can easily confirm the basics--for example, that there is alternating stress as in anɨ́ŋaq 'older brother', anɨ́łxutɨ́kułɨ́ɣi[i]t 'group of brothers', where clearly ɨ can bear stress as well as i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yupik-type iambic rhythm: counting from the left, stress falls on the 2nd syllable and alternate syllables thereafter (schwa may bear stress), with iambic lengthening of open stressed vowels; long vowels (heavy syllables) are stressed and reset the count; closed syllables, initial and non-initial, carry inconsistent extra weight that can attract stress to a closed first syllable or retract/suppress an expected stress after a closed syllable. Krauss's 1990 addendum from direct elicitation (one speaker, 1985) restates it as: stress on any heavy syllable (short closed or long); word-level stress on the 2nd syllable if the 1st is not long, plus on the 1st if it is short closed; no alternating stress beyond the 2nd syllable; and a syntactically conditioned penult stress that is not word-level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Main text: rhythmic alternate-syllable stresses on even-numbered syllables after the 2nd (e.g. aɣyúqiqúvik), often disrupted near closed syllables ('skipping'/retraction). Addendum (verbatim): 'Stress is quite absent on the fourth and eighth syllables, proving the inoperativity of the alternate syllable stress beyond the second syllable' in the speech of the 1985 consultant; no primary/secondary ranking is given in either account.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowel in the 1st syllable takes stress (kēɣniqáquq); fluctuation qantáɣakun ~ qántaɣakun, mantíɣamun ~ mántiɣamun attributed to closed-initial-syllable weight and possibly to dialect mixture within Naukanski (Pouten-Naukan vs Uelen, sec. 3.4); disyllables show 'fairly even weight on both syllables'; no distinctive pre-long-vowel gemination (unlike CAY); overlength contrast possibly lost. Addendum verbatim: 'there are three types of stress placement: 1) general tendency for stress on any heavy syllable (short closed as well as long); 2) stress sometimes on penult, syntactically determined, not word-level stress; 3) word-level stress on second syllable (if first not long), along with the stress on first if short closed.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody inferred philologically from Menovshchikov's (1975) accent marks in texts, paradigms and lexicon plus one tape of connected narrative (Nutetein); Krauss warns the phonetics are 'delicate', affected by unsorted discourse-level factors, and possibly by dialect mixture. The 1990 addendum separates word-level stress (types 1 and 3) from a sentence-level penult stress (type 2), example qiqmíɣaraɣasùxłuraraɣáqa 'my nice poor little doggie'.
new_statements.identity_note: Krauss's 'Naukanski' = Naukan Yupik (nauk1242, East Cape Siberian Yupik), data from Naukan-village speakers recorded by Menovshchikov 1948-1971, an Oslo tape of the narrator Nutetein, and (addendum) speaker Antonina Verbitskaya, Moscow 1985; Krauss suspects internal dialect mixture (Pouten-Naukan vs Uelen varieties). The Menovshchikov 1997 Jazyki mira stress paragraph describes 'Asiatic Eskimo' based mainly on Chaplino (Central Siberian Yupik, cent2128) and must not be used for nauk1242. Glottolog's ref 'Menovshchikov 1980 Jazyk eskimosov Beringova proliva' concerns Big Diomede (Imaklik) Inupiaq, not Naukan.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2-3.4 (pp. 184-188): from Menovshchikov 1975 transcriptions plus an Oslo tape, Naukanski has alternating (iambic, 'fundamentally deuterotonic') stress starting on the 2nd syllable, schwa stressable, perturbed by long vowels; closed initial and non-initial syllables carry inconsistent 'balancing' weight that sometimes attracts/retracts stress (qantáɣakun ~ qántaɣakun); no pre-long gemination (unlike CAY); system 'intermediate between CSY and CAY, basically like CSY'. 1990 addendum (PDF p. 8) from Krauss's Dec 1985 session with speaker A. sources.citation: ru.wikipedia.org, 'Naukanskij jazyk', section 'Udarenie' (accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Second-hand (evidently after Menovshchikov 1975:31-32): stress little studied, two types (expiratory, quantitative); disyllables stressed on the 1st, rarely 2nd (/ˈkamlu/ but /mɨsˈaq/); trisyllables mostly on the 2nd; four-syllable words every other syllable; deviations tied to morpheme semantics. Note the disyllable claim conflicts with Krauss's reading of the same data.

sources.citation: Menovshchikov, G. A. 1997. Aziatskix eskimosov jazyk. In: Jazyki mira: Paleoaziatskie jazyki, 75-81. Moskva: Indrik.
sources.note: p. 76 (sketch explicitly 'based mostly on Chaplino dialect data', Naukan treated as a dialect): 'Udarenie svobodnoe'; disyllables mostly stressed on the 2nd syllable unless the 1st has a long vowel; trisyllables mostly on the 2nd; polysyllables every other syllable from the first stressed one (model 2-4-6 most frequent), counted from a long first vowel if present; a word-medial long vowel breaks the rhythm. No Naukan-specific stress statement; the volume has no separate Naukan entry.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1985. Evolution of prosody in the Yupik languages. In Krauss (ed.) 1985, Yupik Eskimo Prosodic Systems (ANLC Research Papers 7), pp. 135-157 (same PDF).
sources.note: p. 139: 'Rhythmic lengthening also appears to be operative in Naukanski SY.' p. 145: the two CSY foot rules (heavy syllable = foot, stressed; light + following syllable = iambic foot, stress and iambic lengthening on the second) 'are found in some form in all Yupik... Naukanski and BS Inupiaq also share these rules in the same form... in Naukanski we seem to find cases where light closed syllables are defined as monosyllabic feet, although the available data do not allow us to draw definite conclusions'; fn.: Sirenikski and Naukanski 'largely ignored' pending better understanding.
